parts.partTitle: Adapter vs Decorator: The Wrapper War

beats.headline: Adapter and Decorator look the same, but they aren't.
beats.subline: One changes the interface to fix incompatibility, the other stacks behavior.
beats.narration: Adapter and Decorator look identical on a class diagram. Both wrap an object. But their intent is polar opposites. If you mix them up, you'll end up with unmaintainable spaghetti code.

beats.title: Interface Intent

top.label: Adapter
top.code:
interface Target { void execute(); }
class Adapter implements Target { ... }

bottom.label: Decorator
bottom.code:
interface Service { void run(); }
class Decorator implements Service { ... }

beats.narration: Adapter is a translator. It forces a square peg into a round hole by changing the interface. Decorator is an enhancer. It keeps the interface identical while adding layers like logging or retries.

beats.title: Object Adapter Pattern

steps.explanation: The adapter must conform to your domain interface.
Hold the legacy object as a private final field.
Convert domain types (BigDecimal) to legacy types (long).

beats.narration: Use composition, not inheritance, for your adapter. This works even if the legacy class is final. You simply map your clean domain parameters into the messy legacy method signature.

beats.title: Decorator Chain
beats.subtitle: Stacking behaviors at runtime
beats.narration: Decorators are recursive. Each layer delegates to the next. Order matters: wrapping a retry in a logger logs every attempt, but wrapping a logger in a retry logs the total latency.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Facades and the God Class trap →
beats.narration: Mastering these wrappers is the first step to clean architecture. In Part 2, we look at Facades and how to avoid the dreaded God Class.

beats.headline: Is your controller orchestrating five different services?
beats.subline: That's a sign you need a Facade, not more spaghetti code.
beats.narration: If your controller calls inventory, payment, shipping, and audit services just to place an order, you've leaked internal complexity. A Facade hides this mess behind a single, clean entry point.

beats.title: Facade Architecture
beats.subtitle: Simplifying subsystem interaction
beats.narration: The Facade doesn't replace the underlying services. It just provides a higher-level API for common workflows. It's the difference between manual assembly and a single 'Place Order' button.

beats.title: Order Fulfillment Facade

steps.explanation: Inject all necessary services into the facade.
The client only interacts with this single method.
The facade manages the sequence of operations.

beats.narration: The facade coordinates the workflow. It handles the sequence, error checking, and delegation. The client doesn't need to know how the inventory or payment systems work internally.

beats.title: Facade vs God Class

bottom.label: God Class

beats.narration: Don't let your facade become a God Class. If you find yourself writing business logic inside the facade, move it back to the domain services. The facade is a coordinator, not a logic owner.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Proxies and the Spring @Transactional trap →
beats.narration: Facades keep your controllers clean. In Part 3, we dive into Proxies and explain why your Spring transactions might be silently failing.

beats.headline: Why does your @Transactional annotation sometimes just... ignore you?
beats.subline: It's not magic. It's a Proxy pattern failure.
beats.narration: Spring's @Transactional relies on proxies. If you call a transactional method from within the same class, you bypass the proxy entirely. Here is why that happens and how to fix it.

beats.title: Proxy Interception
beats.subtitle: How Spring handles transactions
beats.narration: When you call a service, you're actually hitting a generated proxy class. The proxy starts the transaction, calls your method, and commits. But if you call 'this.method()', you jump straight to the target, skipping the proxy.

beats.title: The Self-Invocation Trap

steps.explanation: Calling 'this' uses the raw object, not the proxy.
The proxy never sees this call, so no transaction starts.

beats.narration: This is the classic Spring bug. Because 'this' points to the raw instance, the proxy logic is never invoked. Always move transactional methods to a separate service bean to ensure the proxy is used.

beats.title: JDK Proxy vs CGLIB
beats.narration: JDK proxies are lightweight but need interfaces. CGLIB generates subclasses at runtime, allowing you to proxy concrete classes. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB for maximum flexibility.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
takeaways: Avoid self-invocation to keep proxies active
CGLIB proxies concrete classes via subclassing
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Composite and tree structures →
beats.narration: Proxies are powerful but tricky. In Part 4, we wrap up with the Composite pattern for handling tree-based hierarchies.

beats.headline: Are you checking 'instanceof' everywhere in your tree logic?
beats.subline: Stop the type-checking madness with the Composite pattern.
beats.narration: If your code has an 'if (node instanceof Directory)' block, you're doing it wrong. Composite lets you treat leaves and containers as the same interface, simplifying your entire tree traversal.

beats.title: Composite Structure
beats.subtitle: Uniform interface for leaves and trees
beats.narration: The key is a shared component interface. Whether it's a single file or a directory of files, the caller just calls 'calculateSize()'. The composite handles the recursion automatically.

beats.title: Uniform Traversal

steps.explanation: Define the operations that apply to both leaves and trees.
Holds a list of the same component interface.
The composite sums up the results of its children.

beats.narration: The recursion is elegant. The composite doesn't care if a child is a file or another directory; it just calls the same interface method. This makes your code infinitely extensible.

beats.title: Safety vs Uniformity

top.label: Interface Uniformity
top.code:
interface Item { void add(Item i); }
// FileItem must throw Exception!

bottom.label: Type Safety
bottom.code:
class Directory { void add(Item i); }
// FileItem doesn't have add()!

beats.narration: Don't put 'add()' in the base interface. It forces leaves to throw exceptions, which is a design smell. Keep mutation methods on the composite class to keep your type system clean.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Composite treats trees and leaves uniformly
Keep mutation methods on the composite class
